Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "Please prepare a practical delivery-day guide for the staff handling the Saturday grocery delivery pilot at the fictional Harbor Lane Cooperative. The guide is for dispatchers and drivers who already know the basic ordering system; focus on coordinating packed orders, communicating with customers, and handling delivery exceptions. Use the details below, keep the language direct and calm, and distinguish confirmed procedures from options that still need a decision. Do not imply that the pilot has already happened or that any unresolved option has been approved. The guide should be useful during a busy shift, not read like a promotional announcement.

Harbor Lane has three buildings: Alder House at 14 Harbor Lane, Birch Court at 18 Harbor Lane, and Cedar Flats at 22 Harbor Lane. Deliveries are scheduled between 9:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. on Saturday. The pilot serves 26 households, but the order count may change until Friday at 6:00 p.m. Each building has a front entrance and a side entrance. The side entrances are usually easier for carrying groceries, but they are not always unlocked. Drivers must not prop open either entrance. There is one passenger lift in each building, and it can be occupied or temporarily out of service. A delivery should be taken to the customer's door only when the customer selected that option; otherwise, the driver should use the designated lobby handoff point.

Orders are packed at the market on Larch Street. Dispatch expects the first completed bags to be ready at 8:30 a.m., though produce packing may run late. Chilled and frozen items are packed in separate insulated totes. The tote labels show the customer's first name, building, and order number; they do not show the full apartment number. The printed order sheet has the apartment number and the customer's selected handoff method. Drivers should compare the order number on the sheet and the tote before leaving the market. If labels do not match, keep the bags together at the market and call the dispatcher rather than guessing. Return any reusable totes to the market after the shift, and note a missing tote on the return sheet.

Customers receive a text when their order is marked ready for dispatch, followed by a message when the driver is close. The dispatcher has asked that arrival messages not promise an exact minute. One customer, Lena Ortiz in Birch Court, wrote, “Please call instead of texting when you're downstairs; my phone barely gets messages in the lift.” Her order notes request a door handoff, but the number to call is listed on the printed sheet rather than on the tote. Two customers have asked for no substitutions. For other orders, staff may offer an available replacement only if the order notes permit it; the customer must agree before the replacement is added. If a customer cannot be reached, do not treat silence as approval. Record the item and contact attempts for the dispatcher to review.

The weather forecast currently mentions a chance of showers after 11:00 a.m. No severe-weather procedure has been issued for this pilot. Keep bags protected from rain while carrying them, and do not leave groceries outside a door unless the customer specifically requested that handoff and the location is safe and dry. If the requested drop-off spot is wet or blocked, contact the customer or dispatcher for direction. For a spill, damaged package, or temperature concern, keep the affected items separate from the rest of the order and report what happened. Do not decide on a refund or promise a replacement; those decisions belong to the customer service lead.

The dispatcher will work from the market office and can be reached on the staff channel or by phone. The customer service lead, Mara Chen, is available by phone from 8:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. The buildings do not have a shared concierge desk. A resident volunteer offered to help guide drivers through the lobby, but their availability has not been confirmed, so the guide should not depend on that offer. Parking is limited along Harbor Lane. Drivers can use the loading space by Alder House for up to ten minutes if it is clear, but it is not reserved. Do not block the marked cycle lane or the fire access. If no safe stopping place is available, circle to the public lot on Dock Street and tell dispatch about the delay.

Please organize the guide into short sections that staff can scan quickly. Include an arrival-and-check-in sequence, a clear handoff process, and a short exception procedure for access problems, customer unavailability, mismatched labels, and damaged or temperature-sensitive items. Include the following numbered section exactly as a decision checklist, while making its wording fit naturally into the guide:
1. Match the order number on the printed sheet to the tote label.
2. Confirm the building and the handoff method before unloading.
3. Contact the dispatcher if an entry point is locked or a label does not match.
4. Record unresolved customer requests and item problems without promising an outcome.

End with a concise list of details the dispatcher should confirm before Friday at 6:00 p.m., such as the final order count and whether any additional building access information is available. Do not add a new delivery window, invent apartment numbers or phone numbers, assign a volunteer a confirmed duty, or create policies that are not stated here. Return only the questions; do not write a script or provide sample answers."}, {"id": "arka-v3-train-prompt-0309", "row_sha256": "6302e4a0ec1e9432e3acb192f78a576f37a23d20b95ea3da3e1096b643b1f712", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
could you make these notes into a customer email draft, for people who had North Basket grocery deliveries in Cedar and Mill wards on tuesday oct 14. it is a local grocery delivery service, not a storewide announcement. the email should explain the late deliveries that evening and say what customers can do if their order is still missing or something arrived in poor condition. i need an actual usable draft with a subject line, but please don't write as if it has already been sent. keep it plain and considerate, not a press release, and don't make the company sound like it knows more than these notes show.

some background in case it helps with the wording: North Basket takes online grocery orders, and customers choose a two-hour delivery window. for this group the windows were 5–7 p.m. and 6–8 p.m. the Cedar and Mill routes were combined that evening, with 42 orders on the route. normal practice is that bags are packed at the North Basket warehouse on Larch Street, checked against the order, and loaded into insulated totes before the van leaves. customers get an app notification when the van is on its way, although the app location can lag behind the driver. don't turn that general background into a claim that every order followed the normal process that night.

what we know about tuesday: dispatch notes say a lane closure near Mercer Bridge was reported at about 4:50 p.m. the road closure is confirmed, but nobody has confirmed the exact time the driver reached it. the map in the delivery app did not show the closure until 6:10 p.m. an operations lead said the route delay was “probably connected to the bridge closure,” and also said the combined route had been busy at loading time. those are possible contributing factors, not a settled explanation. we should explain the disruption without saying the bridge was the only cause or that the app itself caused the delays.

at 8 p.m. dispatch marked 11 of the 42 orders as late. six of those orders were marked delivered between 7:40 and 8:15 p.m. five were still open in the system at 8:20 p.m. we have no later status for those five in these notes, so don't say whether they were eventually delivered or cancelled. the original window for some customers had already ended before the delivery was marked complete. don't call all 11 orders undelivered. there were also two chilled totes still recorded in the van at 8:20 p.m., but the notes don't identify which orders they belonged to or what was inside them.

we have a customer message from 7:52 p.m. that says, “I can see the bags, but the driver is still waiting at the building entrance.” the message doesn't name a building or say whether that order is among the six later marked delivered. another customer wrote, “My delivery was marked complete and nothing is by the door.” support had not matched that message to an order when these notes were collected. include the concern in a general way, don't present either message as proof of what happened to a particular order, and don't quote customers in the email unless there is a real reason. one driver told dispatch, “I’m waiting for access to the next building.” that is the driver's wording, but it doesn't tell us which stop or how long the wait lasted.

support received 17 contacts about the Cedar and Mill deliveries between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m. on tuesday. that is the count in the support log, not a count of all affected customers. the contacts included questions about late arrival, an order marked complete but not found, and concerns about chilled items. no count is available for each type. support is open 7 a.m.–10 p.m. every day. customers can contact support in the app or call the number listed on their order confirmation; ask them to have their order number ready if convenient. don't insert a phone number because none is in the notes.

for the practical part, we can say customers whose order is still missing should check the delivery status in the app and contact support if it has not arrived. customers who find missing items, damaged packaging, or chilled items that no longer feel cold enough should contact support with their order number and a description of the issue. don't tell them to keep or discard food, and don't guarantee a refund, replacement, or delivery-fee credit. no decision about compensation is included here. be clear that support can review the individual order, without promising what the review will decide.

there is a possible numbered section, maybe called “If you still need help,” and keep it short and useful:
1. Check the order status in the North Basket app.
2. If the order is still missing, or if anything is missing or in poor condition, contact support in the app or call the number on the order confirmation.
3. Have the order number ready if you can, and describe what is missing or concerning.

please make the email acknowledge that waiting beyond the selected window is frustrating and apologize for the delay, but don't apologize for food safety harm or say there was an injury, since neither is reported. don't claim every customer had the same experience. mention that the app map showed the closure later than the dispatch report, only if it can be said simply and without making it sound like a complete explanation. don't include the internal count of 17 support contacts or the van's two chilled totes in the customer email; those are background notes, not useful customer instructions. don't invent a new delivery estimate, a cause beyond the notes, an investigation result, or a policy decision. finish with a courteous sign-off from North Basket Customer Support. This is a draft for review, not a statement that the issue has been resolved.", "output": "Draft a customer email for North Basket customers who had grocery deliveries scheduled in Cedar and Mill wards on Tuesday, October 14. Include a subject line. This is a draft for review, not an announcement that has already been sent or a statement that the issue has been resolved. Use a plain, considerate tone rather than a press-release style. Acknowledge that waiting beyond a selected delivery window is frustrating and apologize for the delay. Do not imply that every customer had the same experience.

### Background and confirmed details

North Basket is a local grocery delivery service. Customers place orders online and select a two-hour delivery window. The Cedar and Mill routes were combined on Tuesday, with 42 orders on the route. In normal practice, bags are packed at the North Basket warehouse on Larch Street, checked against the order, and loaded into insulated totes before the van leaves. Customers receive an app notification when the van is on its way, though the app location can lag behind the driver. Do not imply that every order followed the normal process that evening.

Dispatch notes report a lane closure near Mercer Bridge at about 4:50 p.m. The road closure is confirmed, but the exact time the driver reached it is not. The delivery app map did not show the closure until 6:10 p.m. An operations lead said the delay was “probably connected to the bridge closure” and also noted that the combined route had been busy at loading time. Treat these as possible contributing factors, not a settled explanation. Explain the disruption without claiming the bridge was the only cause or that the app caused the delays. You may mention that the app map showed the closure later than the dispatch report, but do so simply and without presenting it as a complete explanation.

At 8 p.m., dispatch marked 11 of the 42 orders late. Six of those orders were marked delivered between 7:40 and 8:15 p.m.; five were still open in the system at 8:20 p.m. The notes contain no later status for those five, so do not say whether they were eventually delivered or cancelled. Some customers’ original windows had ended before their deliveries were marked complete. Do not describe all 11 as undelivered. Two chilled totes were recorded in the van at 8:20 p.m., but the notes do not identify their contents or which orders they belonged to. Keep that internal detail out of the email.

### Customer concerns and support guidance

A customer message at 7:52 p.m. said, “I can see the bags, but the driver is still waiting at the building entrance.” It does not identify the building or establish whether that order was among the six later marked delivered. Another customer wrote, “My delivery was marked complete and nothing is by the door.” Support had not matched that message to an order when the notes were collected. A driver told dispatch, “I’m waiting for access to the next building.” The notes do not identify the stop or how long the wait lasted. Do not use these messages as proof of what happened to a particular order; generally acknowledge concerns about late or apparently completed deliveries instead. There is no need to quote customers in the email.

Support received 17 contacts about Cedar and Mill deliveries between 6 and 9 p.m. Tuesday. This is the number in the support log, not a count of all affected customers. The contacts included questions about late arrivals, orders marked complete but not found, and chilled items; no count is available for each type. Do not include the contact count in the email.

Support is open daily from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. Customers can contact support through the app or call the number on their order confirmation. Do not add a phone number. Ask customers to have their order number ready if convenient. Advise anyone whose order is still missing to check its status in the app and contact support if it has not arrived. Customers who find missing items, damaged packaging, or chilled items that no longer feel cold enough should contact support with their order number and a description of the issue. Do not advise customers to keep or discard food, and do not guarantee a refund, replacement, or delivery-fee credit. No compensation decision is provided. Say that support can review the individual order without promising the outcome.

Include a short, useful numbered section titled “If you still need help”:
1. Check the order status in the North Basket app.
2. If the order is still missing, or if anything is missing or in poor condition, contact support in the app or call the number on the order confirmation.
3. Have the order number ready if you can, and describe what is missing or concerning.

Do not claim food-safety harm or an injury; neither is reported. Do not invent a new delivery estimate, a cause beyond the notes, an investigation result, or a policy decision. End with a courteous sign-off from North Basket Customer Support."}]
